title: Recent Developments in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems along with the Involved Forces for Cancer Cell Separation: A Review

subsections.subsection_title: Liquid Biopsy and Clinical Relevance of CTC Separation in Cancer Diagnostics
subsections.content:
Liquid biopsy has emerged as a transformative paradigm in cancer diagnostics, offering a non-invasive alternative to traditional tissue biopsies by analyzing tumor-derived biomarkers in bodily fluids, particularly blood. Among these biomarkers, circulating tumor cells (CTCs) represent intact malignant cells shed from primary or metastatic tumors, providing direct access to live cancer cells for molecular and phenotypic characterization. The isolation and analysis of CTCs enable real-time monitoring of tumor dynamics, including metastatic progression, clonal evolution, and the emergence of therapeutic resistance, thereby facilitating precision oncology strategies ref [1]. Unlike static tissue biopsies, liquid biopsies permit repeated sampling, allowing for longitudinal assessment of treatment response and disease recurrence with minimal patient burden ref [2]. The clinical utility of CTCs has been demonstrated across multiple cancer types, from breast and prostate to bladder and central nervous system malignancies, where conventional diagnostic methods such as cystoscopy or stereotactic biopsy are invasive or limited by low sensitivity ref [5], ref [6]. Recent advances in microfluidic technologies have significantly improved the efficiency, purity, and throughput of CTC isolation, overcoming challenges posed by their extreme rarity and heterogeneity in peripheral blood ref [3]. Moreover, biophysical properties of CTCs—such as size, deformability, and dielectric behavior—have been leveraged for label-free separation, enhancing capture without reliance on epithelial markers that may be downregulated during epithelial-mesenchymal transition ref [4].

The integration of CTC-based liquid biopsy into clinical workflows holds promise for early detection, risk stratification, and personalized therapy selection. Emerging applications include predicting metastatic potential through CTC enumeration, identifying actionable mutations via single-cell genomic analysis, and guiding adaptive treatment regimens in response to evolving tumor profiles ref [2]. As microfluidic platforms continue to evolve toward clinical translation, standardized protocols and large-scale validation studies are essential to establish CTCs as robust biomarkers in routine oncology practice ref [3]. The broader adoption of liquid biopsy technologies, including CTC isolation, is poised to redefine cancer diagnostics by shifting the focus from reactive to proactive, patient-centered care ref [1].

subsections.subsection_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems for High-Throughput CTC Isolation
subsections.content:
Centrifugal microfluidic systems have emerged as powerful platforms for high-throughput circulating tumor cell (CTC) isolation, leveraging controlled centrifugal forces to achieve label-free, size-based separation directly from whole blood. These systems integrate sample processing, cell enrichment, and waste removal into a single, automated platform, eliminating manual handling and enabling clinical scalability. The 'Centrifuge-on-a-Chip' concept, for instance, replicates benchtop centrifugation using fluidic vortices and inertial effects, enabling continuous enrichment of CTCs at mL/min flow rates without moving parts, thereby facilitating integration into point-of-care diagnostics ref [9]. Building on this, all-in-one centrifugal devices have been developed to achieve size-selective CTC capture with high purity by exploiting differential sedimentation under centrifugal fields, achieving >90% recovery and minimal leukocyte contamination ref [8]. The Vortex technology, while primarily inertial, has been adapted in centrifugal configurations to enhance throughput and purity by combining inertial focusing with microscale vortices, enabling isolation of CTCs from 7.5 mL of blood in under 20 minutes with purities up to 94% ref [10]. Recent advances further integrate deformability-based sorting with centrifugal actuation, allowing separation of CTCs even when size overlap with leukocytes exists, thus broadening applicability across cancer types ref [14]. These systems are particularly advantageous in resource-limited settings due to their low cost, minimal reagent use, and compatibility with portable centrifuges.

The scalability and automation of centrifugal microfluidics make them ideal for clinical translation, with several platforms demonstrating robust performance in patient-derived samples from breast and lung cancer. By coupling centrifugal force with microfluidic channel geometries designed for laminar flow control and particle focusing, these systems achieve high recovery rates while preserving cell viability for downstream molecular analysis. The integration of such platforms into liquid biopsy workflows represents a significant step toward standardized, reproducible CTC isolation for real-time cancer monitoring ref [8]. Ongoing research continues to optimize channel design, rotational speed profiles, and surface functionalization to further enhance specificity and throughput, positioning centrifugal microfluidics as a leading contender for next-generation CTC isolation technologies.

subsections.subsection_title: Integration of Inertial and Hybrid Techniques for Enhanced CTC Capture
subsections.content:
The integration of inertial microfluidics with complementary active techniques has emerged as a powerful strategy to overcome the limitations of size-based separation in circulating tumor cell (CTC) isolation, particularly when CTCs exhibit significant size overlap with white blood cells. Hybrid systems leverage inertial focusing to pre-align cells into predictable lateral positions within microchannels, enabling subsequent active forces—such as acoustophoresis, dielectrophoresis (DEP), or ferrohydrodynamics—to act with enhanced precision and efficiency. For instance, a hybrid acousto-inertial platform employs serpentine channels for inertial focusing followed by standing or traveling surface acoustic waves to separate MCF-7 CTCs from neutrophils, achieving high purity without labels ref [11]. Similarly, inertial-ferrohydrodynamic cell separation (inertial-FCS) combines inertial focusing with magnetic particle-induced hydrodynamic forces to resolve cells differing by only 1–2 μm in diameter, enabling throughput exceeding 100,000 cells per second with high recovery rates ref [12].

Other hybrid designs integrate DEP with inertial flow in zigzag or contraction-expansion geometries to exploit both dielectric properties and size-dependent inertial lift forces. A zigzag channel coupling DEP with Dean and inertial forces successfully separates MDA-231 CTCs from identical-sized WBCs at high Reynolds numbers, demonstrating enhanced resolution through multi-force synergy ref [13]. Likewise, a contraction-expansion inertial-DEP device isolates A549 CTCs from WBCs at 300 μL/min with tunable migration via electrode configuration and voltage, achieving a separation distance of 233.4 μm ref [7]. The serial coupling of multi-orifice flow fractionation (MOFF) with DEP further enhances throughput and purity by first removing bulk RBCs and WBCs via hydrodynamic filtration, followed by precise DEP-based enrichment of CTCs ref [6]. These hybrid architectures represent a paradigm shift toward high-throughput, label-free, and high-resolution CTC capture systems suitable for clinical translation.

subsections.subsection_title: Inertial Microfluidics for Cancer Cell Separation: Principles and Device Designs
subsections.content:
Inertial microfluidics leverages hydrodynamic forces—primarily inertial lift forces and Dean drag forces—to achieve size-based, label-free separation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) without external fields or surface functionalization. In curvilinear channels, such as spirals or wavy geometries, secondary flows induced by channel curvature generate equilibrium focusing positions that are highly dependent on particle size. This principle enables continuous, high-throughput isolation of CTCs from whole blood, as demonstrated in spiral microchannels where 10–20 μm polystyrene particles and cancer cells (e.g., neuroblastoma and glioma) were separated with >80% efficiency and >90% viability ref [22]. The slanted spiral design further enhances separation speed and purity by optimizing the balance between inertial migration and Dean flow, achieving ultra-fast CTC isolation from diluted blood samples ref [19].

Recent innovations have expanded device versatility: serial reverse wavy channels enable sheathless focusing of particles as small as 3 μm, facilitating direct CTC sorting from undiluted blood with 89.7% recovery and 68.9% enrichment ref [17]. Contraction-expansion array (CEA) devices operate at low Reynolds numbers to minimize shear stress while maintaining throughput of 1.1×10⁸ cells/min, achieving 99.1% CTC recovery from whole blood (Hct ~45%) ref [16]. Hybrid approaches, such as coupling inertial focusing with deterministic lateral displacement, improve precision by combining size-dependent migration with lateral displacement thresholds ref [8]. Integrated vortex-based systems enable double sorting, purifying cancer stem-like cells from blood with >90% efficiency and 1,500× purity enhancement ref [15]. Comprehensive reviews highlight the evolution of channel topologies—including Archimedean spirals, zigzags, and multi-orifice designs—toward scalable, clinical-grade CTC isolation ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Centrifugal Microvalving and Flow Control Strategies
subsections.content:
Centrifugal microfluidic systems rely on precise flow control strategies to enable complex, automated workflows without external pumps. Passive valving, particularly capillary burst valves, has been foundational in early platforms, leveraging surface tension to gate flow until a threshold centrifugal force is exceeded, as demonstrated in the Bio-Disk platform and microfabricated enzymatic assay systems. However, recent advances have introduced active and hybrid control mechanisms to overcome limitations in timing and reusability. Notably, the Coriolis pseudo-force has been harnessed to create frequency-dependent transversal flow switches, where rotation direction and speed dictate flow diversion into symmetric outlets, enabling dynamic routing without mechanical components. This approach, validated through CFD simulations and experiments, offers a purely inertial, non-contact switching mechanism beyond a threshold of ~350 rad s⁻¹.

To enhance versatility and speed, optically triggered microvalves using nanoheaters embedded in paraffin wax have been developed, allowing rapid (<0.5 s), multiplexed, and spatially selective valve actuation via low-intensity laser illumination. This method enables sequential fluidic operations on a single disk with minimal footprint and high leak resistance (up to 403 kPa). Furthermore, modern centrifugal platforms now integrate pneumatic energy storage and reagent pre-storage units, facilitating complex, multi-step process chains with pulse-free, inertia-driven flow. These innovations, collectively advancing the unit operation library, have positioned centrifugal microfluidics as a robust platform for fully integrated diagnostic systems, particularly in point-of-care and high-throughput applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Circulating Tumor Cell (CTC) Isolation via Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.content:
Centrifugal microfluidic systems have emerged as powerful platforms for the label-free, high-purity isolation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from whole blood, leveraging centrifugal force to exploit physical differences such as size, density, and sedimentation behavior. One notable advancement is the all-in-one centrifugal device that enables size-selective CTC capture with high purity by integrating multiple unit operations on a single disc, eliminating the need for external pumps or complex fluidic interfaces ref [7]. To address the challenge of processing large clinical blood volumes, a fully automated lab-on-a-disc platform has been developed that handles up to 5 mL of whole blood, utilizing a triangular obstacle structure to direct flow and anti-EpCAM-coated microbeads to enhance density-based separation via a density gradient medium, achieving high recovery and purity suitable for downstream molecular analysis ref [28]. More recently, continuous centrifugal microfluidics (CCM) has been introduced to isolate heterogeneous CTC populations under fully automated, high-throughput conditions, enabling real-time processing without sample pre-treatment and demonstrating robust performance across diverse cancer types ref [29].

These systems often integrate inertial focusing, sedimentation, and hydrodynamic sorting mechanisms tuned by rotational speed and disc geometry, allowing for precise control over cell trajectories. The combination of centrifugal force with surface functionalization or density-based media significantly enhances specificity against leukocyte contamination, a persistent challenge in CTC isolation. Moreover, the scalability and compatibility of centrifugal platforms with standard clinical workflows make them particularly attractive for point-of-care liquid biopsy applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Integrated On-Disk Assays: From Cell Lysis to Molecular Detection
subsections.content: Integrated centrifugal microfluidic platforms have enabled fully automated sample-to-answer workflows for nucleic acid analysis, seamlessly combining cell lysis, nucleic acid extraction, amplification, and detection on a single disc. Early demonstrations established mechanical lysis via bead-mediated disruption under centrifugal rimming flow, achieving ~65% efficiency comparable to conventional methods and paving the way for integrated diagnostics ref [30]. Subsequent advances introduced chemically and physically triggered lysis mechanisms, such as laser-irradiated Ferrowax microvalves enabling on-demand release of magnetic beads for pathogen-specific DNA extraction from whole blood within 12 minutes, eliminating manual intervention ref [31]. Thermoplastic elastomer (TPE)-based Lab-on-Disc systems further extended integration by incorporating PCR amplification, amplicon digestion, and microarray hybridization in a monolithic polymer platform, demonstrating robust fluidic control through capillary valves and precise timing ref [32]. To enhance automation of particle-based workflows, centrifugo-pneumatic strategies have been developed to enable sedimentation, supernatant removal (>99.5% efficiency), and re-suspension of microparticles solely via controlled rotational speed changes, without external magnets or surface modifications ref [33]. These innovations collectively address key bottlenecks in point-of-care diagnostics by minimizing user steps, reducing contamination risks, and enabling rapid, reproducible molecular detection directly from complex biological samples such as whole blood.

subsections.subsection_title: Multiplexed Cell and Particle Manipulation in Centrifugal Platforms
subsections.content:
Centrifugal microfluidic platforms have emerged as powerful tools for multiplexed manipulation of cells and particles, leveraging controlled inertial and sedimentation forces to achieve high-throughput, parallelized processing. Array-based trapping architectures, such as V-cup geometries, enable precise capture and spatial distribution of beads or cells via stopped-flow sedimentation under centrifugal fields, achieving near-100% capture efficiency and single-occupancy distributions critical for digital readouts in multiplexed assays. This approach facilitates simultaneous color- or fluorescence-coded analysis of multiple biomolecular targets on a single disk, significantly reducing instrument complexity and enabling point-of-care diagnostics. Beyond beads, such platforms have been extended to isolate and cultivate single cells, as demonstrated by microchamber arrays that trap individual cells—such as Jurkat and NIH3T3 lines—under centrifugal flow, allowing for longitudinal monitoring of proliferation without medium exchange. The integration of hydrodynamic focusing, sedimentation gradients, and centrifugal valve actuation further permits sequential, multiplexed operations including sorting, washing, and lysis within a single platform.

Recent innovations have expanded these capabilities to include label-free, size- and deformability-based multiplexing of heterogeneous cell populations, enabling concurrent isolation of distinct subpopulations from complex samples like whole blood. By tuning rotational speed and channel geometry, centrifugal forces can be harnessed to partition cells into multiple output streams, each dedicated to a specific target population. These systems are particularly advantageous for cancer diagnostics, where parallel processing of CTCs, leukocytes, and other circulating elements enhances diagnostic yield and reduces sample handling time.

subsections.subsection_title: Centrifugal Force-Driven Blood Separation and Plasma Extraction
subsections.content:
Centrifugal force-driven plasma extraction from whole blood is a cornerstone of point-of-care diagnostic platforms, enabling rapid, automated sample preparation without external pumps or complex instrumentation. Early demonstrations established the feasibility of decanting plasma from sedimented cellular layers using precisely controlled rotational speeds, achieving high-purity plasma yields (e.g., 2 µL from 5 µL whole blood) within seconds at moderate frequencies (40 Hz), with residual cell contamination below 0.11% ref [37]. Subsequent innovations introduced microfluidic valving mechanisms to enhance control and purity; out-of-plane microvalves, for instance, physically isolate plasma in an upstream reservoir from sedimented cells, achieving 99.9% plasma purity and 96 ± 0.5% yield by preventing back-diffusion during spin cycles ref [39]. A more recent advancement employs centrifugo-pneumatic gating, where pressure-induced deflection of a liquid membrane regulates flow initiation after sedimentation, eliminating the need for surface functionalization or hybrid materials and simplifying fabrication ref [36]. These strategies are further refined in integrated lab-on-CD systems that combine plasma separation with downstream metering and splitting, enabling precise volumetric control (±0.5 nL) and compatibility with quantitative assays such as creatinine detection across a broad hematocrit range (6–48%) ref [5].

The integration of these separation techniques with on-disk processing units has enabled fully automated workflows, from whole blood input to analyte detection, significantly reducing manual intervention and sample loss. The scalability and reproducibility of centrifugal plasma extraction make it particularly suitable for resource-limited settings, where portability and low cost are paramount. Ongoing research continues to optimize sedimentation kinetics, channel geometry, and rotational profiles to maximize yield and purity while minimizing hemolysis and processing time.

subsections.subsection_title: Forces in Rotational Microfluidic Platforms - Subtopic 1
subsections.content: In rotational microfluidic platforms, the separation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from blood is governed by a complex interplay of inertial, centrifugal, and drag forces, which are modulated by cell size, density, and deformability. Centrifugal force dominates in rotating systems, enabling size-based segregation where larger CTCs migrate outward more strongly than smaller blood cells, as demonstrated in high-speed disk-based platforms. However, recent studies highlight that CTCs do not behave as isolated entities; their interaction with platelets, neutrophils, and macrophages significantly alters their effective hydrodynamic properties and escape dynamics under rotational shear. For instance, CTC-platelet aggregates exhibit enhanced resistance to centrifugal displacement due to increased effective size and altered surface rheology, complicating pure size-based separation strategies ref [40]. Moreover, the viscoelastic nature of blood plasma and the presence of fibrin networks induced by activated platelets can shield CTCs from dominant centrifugal forces, necessitating hybrid approaches that account for these biological interactions. The balance between centrifugal force and viscous drag is further influenced by rotational frequency and channel geometry, where optimal design must mitigate shear-induced cell damage while maximizing separation efficiency.

subsections.subsection_title: Density Gradient-Based Cell Separation in Centrifugal Systems
subsections.content:
Density gradient-based centrifugal separation has emerged as a powerful label-free strategy for isolating rare cancer cells from whole blood by exploiting intrinsic density differences between cellular components. Recent advances in centrifugal microfluidics have enabled the integration of discrete, continuous density gradients within a single rotating disk, allowing simultaneous fractionation of blood into multiple layers—enriching leukocytes, platelets, and plasma while retaining nucleated tumor cells in targeted zones. Ref [1] demonstrated a microfluidic platform capable of separating ~5 µL whole blood samples into removable fractions using engineered density interfaces, facilitating on-disk leukocyte enrichment for microscopy and downstream analysis. This approach leverages centrifugal forces to drive sedimentation and stratification, minimizing shear-induced cell damage compared to inertial methods. Subsequent studies have refined gradient materials and channel geometries to enhance resolution and reproducibility, enabling separation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from mononuclear cells with high purity and recovery rates. The scalability and automation potential of these systems make them ideal for point-of-care diagnostics, particularly when integrated with on-chip staining or molecular detection modules.

Further innovations include the use of biocompatible density media such as iodixanol and Percoll analogs, optimized for microfluidic flow dynamics and compatible with low-volume samples. These systems have been extended to isolate CTCs from metastatic cancer patients with high specificity, outperforming conventional Ficoll-based methods in throughput and reproducibility. Integration with pneumatic valves and optical readouts has enabled fully automated, multi-step workflows from sample input to analysis, reducing manual intervention and contamination risks. The modularity of centrifugal platforms also permits sequential density-based separations, allowing for multi-stage purification of heterogeneous cell populations. As such, density gradient centrifugation on microfluidic discs represents a robust, clinically translatable paradigm for liquid biopsy applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Size-Selective Isolation of Circulating Tumor Cells (CTCs)
subsections.content:
Size-selective isolation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) leverages the distinct physical dimensions of CTCs relative to blood cells, enabling label-free, high-purity separation in centrifugal microfluidic systems. Centrifugal forces enhance hydrodynamic focusing and size-based discrimination, allowing CTCs—typically larger than leukocytes and erythrocytes—to be routed into dedicated outlet channels via strategically designed spiral or radial microchannels. Recent advances have integrated inertial focusing with deterministic lateral displacement (DLD) on centrifugal platforms, achieving precise size-based sorting with minimal shear stress and high throughput. For instance, a centrifugal microfluidic device employing a serpentine channel array successfully isolated CTCs from whole blood with >85% recovery and >90% purity by exploiting size-dependent inertial lift forces ref [35]. Other systems utilize multi-orifice flow fractionation under centrifugal actuation to separate CTCs based on their hydrodynamic diameter, demonstrating compatibility with clinical sample volumes ref [15].

Further innovations include the coupling of centrifugal sedimentation with microfiltration membranes or size-tuned obstacles, enabling continuous, automated CTC capture without external pumps. These platforms often integrate on-chip sample preparation, reducing pre-processing steps and enhancing point-of-care applicability. Notably, devices incorporating variable rotational speeds allow dynamic tuning of effective centrifugal forces to accommodate heterogeneous CTC populations, improving capture efficiency across epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) states ref [12]. The scalability and automation of such systems make them particularly suitable for liquid biopsy workflows, where reproducibility and minimal sample handling are critical. Recent studies have validated these approaches using clinical samples from breast, lung, and prostate cancer patients, confirming high concordance with traditional immunomagnetic methods ref [36].

subsections.subsection_title: Integrated Centrifugal Platforms for Immune and Cancer Cell Sorting
subsections.content: Integrated centrifugal platforms have emerged as powerful tools for simultaneous sorting of immune and cancer cells from complex biological samples, leveraging multiplexed fluidic architectures and automated on-chip processing. Recent advances have enabled the co-isolation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and key immune subsets—such as T cells, monocytes, and neutrophils—within a single disc-based system, facilitating comprehensive liquid biopsy analysis. One notable platform utilizes centrifugal force-driven density stratification coupled with inertial focusing and hydrodynamic sorting to achieve label-free separation of CTCs from leukocytes in whole blood, achieving high purity and recovery rates ref [42]. These systems often integrate multiple unit operations, including sample dilution, cell focusing, and fraction collection, all controlled by precise rotational profiles, minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility. Furthermore, hybrid designs incorporating pneumatic valves and optical triggers allow dynamic reconfiguration of flow paths for adaptive sorting based on cell phenotype or size, enabling personalized diagnostic workflows. The scalability and compatibility of such platforms with downstream molecular assays make them ideal for point-of-care applications in cancer immunotherapy monitoring and metastatic progression tracking.

subsections.subsection_title: Centrifugal Plasma Extraction for Cancer Diagnostics
subsections.content:
Centrifugal plasma extraction has emerged as a critical enabler for point-of-care cancer diagnostics, providing rapid, automated isolation of plasma from whole blood for downstream molecular analysis. The technique leverages centrifugal force to sediment blood cells, enabling passive separation of plasma through decanting structures or gated flow channels. Early work by Haeberle et al. demonstrated efficient extraction of 2 µL plasma from 5 µL whole blood within 20 seconds at 40 Hz, achieving residual cell concentrations below 0.11%, thereby ensuring high plasma purity essential for reliable biomarker detection ref [37]. Subsequent innovations introduced centrifugo-pneumatic gating mechanisms that precisely control flow initiation via pressure-induced membrane deflection, eliminating the need for surface functionalization or hybrid materials and simplifying device fabrication ref [36]. These platforms enable metered plasma delivery directly to integrated assay zones for PCR, immunoassays, or nucleic acid extraction, facilitating fully automated liquid biopsy workflows. The compatibility of such systems with standard lab-on-a-disc architectures allows seamless coupling with downstream cancer biomarker detection modules, including ctDNA analysis and protein profiling. Recent advances have further improved throughput and reproducibility by optimizing disc geometry, rotational profiles, and interfacial tension control, making centrifugal plasma extraction a robust, scalable solution for clinical translation.

Beyond the foundational designs, newer implementations integrate real-time monitoring and adaptive spin protocols to accommodate variable hematocrit levels, enhancing reliability across diverse patient populations. The modularity of these systems supports multiplexed diagnostics, enabling simultaneous extraction and analysis of multiple cancer-related analytes from a single drop of blood. As such, centrifugal plasma extraction is no longer merely a preparatory step but a core component of integrated diagnostic platforms poised to transform non-invasive cancer monitoring.
